passage: Artificial light at night has transformed modern cities, extending productive hours and enhancing street safety. Yet chronobiologists warn that widespread nighttime illumination disrupts a fundamental biological rhythm shared by nearly all organisms: the circadian clock. In humans, exposure to blue-rich light from screens and LED streetlights after sunset suppresses the secretion of melatonin, a hormone that regulates sleep onset and cellular repair. Beyond causing chronic sleep deprivation, circadian disruption has been linked to metabolic disorders, weakened immunity, and impaired cognitive performance. Wildlife suffers as well, as migratory birds become disoriented by illuminated skyscrapers and sea turtle hatchlings crawl toward coastal lights instead of the ocean. Adopting warmer-spectrum bulbs, shielded outdoor fixtures, and screen-free evening routines can preserve the benefits of modern lighting while protecting biological rhythms.
